passage: Sumit, you say a man in a crisp uniform and a lanyard came to your flat asking to check the meter and for your card details? Hear what happened to me. I'm Mridul. At twenty-five a man in a khaki shirt and a badge rang my bell and said he was from the power company and needed my bill and an OTP to "fix an error." The uniform looked right and my first thought was to trust him. But something nagged me: a real officer wouldn't need an OTP. I said, "Please wait, I'll call the power company's number from my bill." He said he'd come back later and left quickly. The helpline confirmed no visit was planned. Anyone can buy a shirt and print a badge. Check through the official number, not the one they give you.

qa.q: What did the man ask Mridul for besides checking the meter?
qa.a: Mridul's bill and an OTP.

qa.q: What was Mridul thinking when the man asked for an OTP?
qa.a: Something nagged at Mridul, since a real officer wouldn't need an OTP, even though the uniform looked right and Mridul's first thought was to trust it.

qa.q: What should Sumit do now?
qa.a: Sumit should not share details, check through the official number on the bill or website, and tell a trusted person.

qa.q: How might the man have reacted to Mridul's plan to call?
qa.a: He left quickly, which suggests he did not want the check, though that is not proof.

grounding: A uniform and badge signal a role, but identity must be verified through the official channel because anyone can wear a costume.

passage: Rain was pouring and the lobby was closing in ten minutes when a man in a delivery uniform and a lanyard hurried to Tanvir's security desk. "Urgent parcel for the sixth floor, Damini Rao. I have to hand it to her myself," he said, dripping. The uniform looked right and the man looked tired, and Tanvir felt a pull to wave him through. Instead he said, "Sorry, I'll call her first." He dialled Damini's extension. "A parcel?" she said. "I didn't order anything. Don't send him up; I'll come down." The man said, "Never mind, wrong address," and walked back into the rain. Tanvir didn't know whether the man had been a scammer or just mistaken. He wrote the time and description in the visitor log.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do first at the desk?
qa.a: He said he would call Damini first, then dialled her extension.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he saw the man in the delivery uniform?
qa.a: He felt a pull to wave him through, out of sympathy for a tired, wet man, but he still chose to check.

qa.q: Why was calling Damini a good step?
qa.a: It verified the claim through a proper channel, since anyone can wear a uniform.

qa.q: How might the delivery man have felt when he was refused?
qa.a: Perhaps frustrated or embarrassed, or simply mistaken; Tanvir could not tell.

grounding: A young professional reads a uniform and lanyard as a signal of role but verifies through the proper channel despite time pressure and bad weather.

passage: At four on a Tuesday, the doorbell of Sonali and Dilnaz's flat in Kothrud rang. A man in a khaki uniform, with an electricity board badge on a lanyard, said the meter inside needed urgent checking. "Five minutes, madam. There's a fault in the building." The uniform looked real. The badge had a photo. Dilnaz was already reaching for the latch. Sonali stopped her hand. "Let me just check." She kept the chain on and said politely, "Please wait. I'll call the office." She rang the board's official helpline number from the bill on the fridge, then the society's security desk downstairs. The board had no visit scheduled. The guard said no electricity staff had signed in. When Sonali opened the door again, the man was gone. The guard came up and took their description, and the society secretary sent a warning to every flat that evening.

qa.q: Which two places did Sonali call?
qa.a: The electricity board's official helpline and the society's security desk.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she reached for the latch?
qa.a: Dilnaz seemed trusting and reassured by the real-looking uniform and badge, wanting to be helpful.

qa.q: Why was Sonali's check the right step?
qa.a: A uniform and badge can be faked, so verifying through the official helpline and security desk before opening the door protected them.

qa.q: How did the society respond after the incident?
qa.a: The guard took their description, and the secretary sent a warning to every flat that evening.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a uniform and badge as a claim of authority and verifying through proper channels before trusting it.

passage:
"Records for Bed 12, please," said the man in the white coat, leaning on the ward counter. "Dr. Menon asked me to collect them."
Chetan, three weeks into his job as ward clerk, reached for the file. Kavitha, the senior nurse, put a hand on the folder.
"Sorry, Doctor, I don't think we've met. Which department?"
"Cardiology. New registrar." He tapped the stethoscope round his neck. "I'm in a bit of a rush."
"Of course. Could I see your hospital ID card?"
He patted his pockets. "Left it in the car."
"No problem. Chetan, could you call the cardiology office and confirm, please?"
Chetan dialled. The secretary said there was no new registrar, and Dr. Menon was on leave. When he turned back, the man was walking quickly toward the stairs.
Kavitha was already on the phone to security. "Man in a white coat, grey trousers, heading down the east stairs."
Chetan's hands were cold. "He looked exactly like a doctor."
"That's the point," Kavitha said. "A coat is just a coat."

qa.q: Which bed's records did the man ask for?
qa.a: Bed 12.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after the man walked off?
qa.a: Chetan felt shaken, hands cold, realising how convincingly the man had looked like a doctor.

qa.q: What steps did Kavitha take to verify identity?
qa.a: She politely asked which department, asked for his hospital ID card, had Chetan call the cardiology office, and alerted security when he walked off.

qa.q: How did Kavitha read the white coat?
qa.a: Kavitha treated it as a signal to check, not proof, knowing that 'a coat is just a coat'.

grounding: Shows a young clerk reading a white coat as authority and a senior nurse verifying identity through proper channels.

passage: In my first month as a constable in Guwahati, I stopped a car at a night checkpoint, and the young woman driving, Aditi, wouldn't roll her window down more than an inch. "Can I see your ID, please? And I'd like to call the control room to confirm this checkpoint." I'll admit, my first feeling was irritation. I was in full uniform, with a badge, under a streetlight. Who did she think I was? But my senior, standing behind me, nodded at her. "Of course, madam. Call 112. Binita, hold up your ID." She did, gave our location, and the control room confirmed. Only then did she lower her window. Driving home that night, I thought about why she'd done it. There had been reports that month of fake uniforms stopping women on the highway. To her, my uniform was a costume until proven otherwise. She was right. Now I hold my ID up before anyone asks, and tell people they can call to check. It makes my work easier, not harder.

qa.q: Where did Binita work as a constable?
qa.a: In Guwahati.

qa.q: What was Binita's first feeling when Aditi asked for ID?
qa.a: Binita felt irritated, thinking the uniform and badge should have been enough.

qa.q: What does Binita now do differently, and why?
qa.a: Binita holds up the ID before anyone asks and tells people they can call to check, because uniforms can be faked and verification builds trust.

qa.q: Why did Aditi insist on verifying?
qa.a: Aditi was cautious because fake uniforms had been used to stop women that month, so she treated the uniform as unproven until the control room confirmed.

grounding: A young constable recalls a driver verifying a uniform through the control room and coming to value checks because anyone can wear a costume.

passage:
Office manager's note, Tuesday
At about 3 pm a man in a blue uniform with a lanyard came to reception and told Anand he was from the building's fire-safety contractor, there to check the server room extinguishers. He was confident and in a hurry. The badge looked real enough.
Anand told me later his first instinct was to wave him through. Instead he said, politely, "Sure, one moment, I just need to confirm with facilities," and called the number on our own contractor list, not the number on the man's card. Facilities had no visit booked.
When Anand turned back, the man had already walked out.
Ankita, at the next desk, pointed out that the lanyard's logo was slightly wrong. We have reported it to building security and the police, and shared his description with the other offices in the building.
Anand did exactly what we trained for: a uniform tells you someone wants to look official, not that they are.

qa.q: What did the man say he was there to check?
qa.a: The server room extinguishers.

qa.q: What does Anand's first instinct suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Wanting to wave the man through suggests Anand felt reassured, and perhaps a little pressured, by the confident manner, uniform and hurry.

qa.q: How did Anand check the visitor?
qa.a: He politely said he needed to confirm, and called facilities on the number from the office's own contractor list, not the man's card.

qa.q: What did Ankita notice that others might have missed?
qa.a: Ankita noticed that the lanyard's logo was slightly wrong.

grounding: A young professional reads a uniform and badge as a claim of authority and verifies it through proper channels, since anyone can wear a costume.
